## 80,000 trees to be planted to support Koala conservation

## A wildlife corridor is only as wide as its narrowest point
https://elyciap.github.io/fnpw-website-2026/article-a-wildlife-corridor-is-only-as-wide-as-its-narrowest-point.html

Urban sprawl rarely wipes out a wildlife corridor outright, it pinches it. Four fast-growing regions show what width, continuity and permanence decide.
Urban sprawl rarely wipes out a wildlife corridor outright. It pinches them: a subdivision here, a road widening there, a reserve that takes decades to fully secure. Australia is good at identifying the corridors that matter. The harder part, the part that decides whether a population holds on, is delivering them at the width, length and permanence that actually works. Four of the country’s fastest growing regions show what that gap looks like on the ground, and what closes it.

## Browsers, not just grazers
https://elyciap.github.io/fnpw-website-2026/article-browsers-not-just-grazers.html

Wallabies browse foliage and young bark, not just grass. How one revegetation project found an effective, economical tree guard after years of losses.
A government adviser said not to use tree-guards in our revegetation; we had de-stocked and rabbits, hares or wallabies would graze on kikuyu, not seedlings. We planted 100 tubes with care, but without tree-guards. It was soon obvious the seedlings were being munched to the ground and most were killed. Red-necked and swamp wallabies were eating trees as fast as we could plant them.

## Bushfire Recovery Partnership

## Fire Wise Australia
https://elyciap.github.io/fnpw-website-2026/article-fire-wise-project-lanscape-resilience.html

It’s a movement that’s not only redefining bushfire preparedness but also enhancing local biodiversity through strategic planting of appropriate native species. With a focus on three crucial aspects of bushfires, the project is igniting a new era of safety and conservation.

## Fire Wise Project
https://elyciap.github.io/fnpw-website-2026/article-fire-wise-project.html

Our Fire Wise project helps communities in the Bega Valley, East Gippsland and the Adelaide Hills to Kangaroo Island corridor reduce bushfire risk.
As part of the Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife (FNPW) Landscape Resilience Program the Fire Wise project will be delivered in 10 key Local Government Areas across the Bega Valley, New South Wales; East Gippsland, Victoria; and the Adelaide Hills to Kangaroo Island corridor in South Australia. The aim of the project is to help communities mitigate bushfire risk through community-based natural resource management initiatives.

## Frog Disease
https://elyciap.github.io/fnpw-website-2026/article-frog-disease.html

Frogs are known and celebrated for their disease resistance abilities. However, they are currently facing a global pandemic of their own.
Frogs are known and celebrated for their disease resistance abilities. However, they are currently facing a global pandemic of their own. Chytrid fungus (Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis) that causes the disease chytridiomycosis has decimated many frog populations worldwide. It is known to have affected frogs in eastern Australia and has likely caused local extinctions and ongoing declines of many species.

## Protecting Bilbies through right-way fire management in the Kimberley
https://elyciap.github.io/fnpw-website-2026/article-protecting-bilbies-through-right-way-fire-management-in-the-kimberley.html

Environs Kimberley supports Aboriginal Rangers around Fitzroy Crossing to document bilbies and manage wrong-way fire, with new funding from us.
Unlike many places in Australia, the Greater Bilby (Macrotis lagotis) is still present in the Kimberley in Western Australia due to no or lower densities of rabbits and foxes, and ongoing management by Aboriginal rangers. This makes it an important wild refugia in Australia. Unfortunately, bilbies are still threatened in the region by habitat changes resulting from wrong-way fire, land-clearing and over-grazing.

## Three key takeaways for mitigating the effects of environmental change on Australia’s fragile ecosystem
https://elyciap.github.io/fnpw-website-2026/article-takeaways-for-mitigating-effects.html

Australia's ecosystems face unprecedented pressure from environmental change. Three key takeaways from our eBook on how we can help change the course.
Australia’s unique ecosystem has shown remarkable resilience over time yet is now facing unprecedented challenges due to the persistent impact of human-induced environmental change. Catastrophic natural disasters, such as devastating floods, damaging cyclones, record-breaking droughts, and raging bushfires, have become increasingly frequent, causing widespread damage to the country’s valuable natural resources.

## The Bandicoot: A Little Gardener Beneath Our Feet
https://elyciap.github.io/fnpw-website-2026/article-the-bandicoot-a-little-gardener-beneath-our-feet.html

One southern brown bandicoot turns close to four tonnes of soil a year. Why this shy digger matters, and how the Bandicoot Superhighway helps it.
In the underbrush of Australia’s south and southeast, a small, shy marsupial is quietly performing some of the most important work in our ecosystems. The Southern Brown Bandicoot (Isoodon obesulus) may not have the fame of kangaroos or koalas, but when it comes to ecological impact, this little digger is a heavyweight.

## Trees planted in McCullys Gap

We had a great day on Tuesday June 14th, planting trees in the Youngman Creek rehabilitation corridor. About 30 of us met and yarned about what’s going on at Namabunda. We cleared another 300 square metres of degraded creek line and created a rehabilitation area with an initial planting of 45 plants.

## Upper Shoalhaven Landcare’s Trees for Ongoing Disaster Recovery
https://elyciap.github.io/fnpw-website-2026/article-usl-trees.html

Our Bushfire Recovery grant helped Upper Shoalhaven Landcare distribute 1,500 native tubestock across 17 sites and hold two community plantings in Araluen.
The Bushfire Recovery grant for Upper Shoalhaven Landcare was used to support ongoing disaster recovery and revegetation efforts across our Landcare network in the Queanbeyan-Palerang Council Region. Overall 1500 native tubestock, 1100 stakes, 600 guards, 500 jute mesh squares, fertilizer and catering for 2 community tree-planting events were purchased and distributed across 17 sites across Bombay, Braidwood, Bendoura, Mongarlowe and Araluen.

Warddeken Rangers and the Karrkad Kanjdji Trust are working to protect vulnerable Mayh (species/animals) in the Stone Country of west Arnhem Land. Every donation is put to work across our three pillars, funding conservation projects Australia-wide with First Nations groups, rangers and scientists.
Every donation is put to work across our three pillars. Here is what that looks like.

## Keeping Australia wild since 1970
https://elyciap.github.io/fnpw-website-2026/

We grow national parks, save threatened species and heal damaged country. The Foundation for National Parks & Wildlife, since 1970.
We bring First Nations organisations, government, communities and funders together to protect Australia’s most important landscapes and wildlife, from first opportunity to measurable impact.

Talking wildlife, national parks or one of our projects? We can help with interviews, imagery and background.

## Cultivating Koala Habitat
https://elyciap.github.io/fnpw-website-2026/project-cultivating-koala-habitat.html

With Wollondilly Shire Council we restored four hectares of koala habitat corridor along the Bargo River: 2,000 local plants, 95 per cent still alive.
The first koala a European ever wrote down was seen on the Bargo River in 1798. Two centuries later, a nursery run largely by the people who live there is growing the trees that will keep koalas on the same stretch of water.

## Garner's Beach Cassowary Rehabilitation Centre Project
https://elyciap.github.io/fnpw-website-2026/project-garners-beach-cassowary-rehabilitation-centre-project.html

The Garner's Beach Cassowary Rehabilitation Centre has cared for sick, injured and orphaned Southern Cassowaries, an endangered species, since 2001.
In Australia, the Cassowary is listed as endangered with numbers at around 1,500 to 2,000. But these are guesstimates; no one knows for sure. That’s because Cassowaries live alone in dense forests and they’re hard to count. Cassowary males and females look pretty much the same when they’re young, but females eventually grow about a foot taller, reaching some six feet. They start breeding at age four or five and can live 40 years or more.

## Genetic Code of Koalas
https://elyciap.github.io/fnpw-website-2026/project-genetic-code-of-koalas.html

We funded the Australian Museum to read the DNA of koalas around Port Macquarie and find out whether they were still reaching each other.
You cannot protect a population you cannot tell apart from the next one. We funded the Australian Museum to read the DNA of koalas on the New South Wales mid-north coast and find out whether they were still reaching each other.

## Kaurna Cultural Fire at Kauwi-marnirla
https://elyciap.github.io/fnpw-website-2026/project-kaurna-cultural-fire-field-river.html

Kaurna-led cultural fire at Kauwi-marnirla (Field River) in Adelaide's south, backed by $4.07 million from the Disaster Ready Fund, led by Kaurna Kardla.
Kaurna fire practitioners are caring for Country with cultural fire again, in a valley ringed by Adelaide’s southern suburbs. Backed by $4.07 million from the Australian Government’s Disaster Ready Fund, the work began with Firesticks and is now led by Kaurna Kardla, a Kaurna organisation in its own right.

## Saving Species
https://elyciap.github.io/fnpw-website-2026/saving-species.html

We protect Australia's most vulnerable species by restoring habitat, creating wildlife corridors and supporting recovery programs across the country.
We protect Australia's most vulnerable species by restoring habitats, creating wildlife corridors, and supporting targeted conservation programs.

## Give your team a day to bring back the bush.
https://elyciap.github.io/fnpw-website-2026/volunteer.html

Corporate volunteering days in national parks, nurseries and wetlands across Australia. Give your team a hands-on day restoring habitat.
Australia is home to plants and animals found nowhere else on Earth, and your team can play a practical part in protecting them. Step away from the office for a hands-on day outdoors, working together alongside our rangers and community nurseries to care for places that need it.

However you want to help, there is a way that fits. Four ways to give, four ways to give time and influence. Choose yours.

## Why your support matters.
https://elyciap.github.io/fnpw-website-2026/why-your-support-is-needed.html

Australia is home to species found nowhere else, and one of the worst extinction records on Earth. Your support is not optional; it is the whole mechanism.
Australia is home to species found nowhere else, and one of the worst extinction records on Earth. Support is not optional; it is the whole mechanism.

## Workplace giving.
https://elyciap.github.io/fnpw-website-2026/workplace-giving.html

A small amount from each pay, before tax, often matched by your employer. Set and forget, and it adds up to habitat for our native wildlife.
A small amount from each pay, before tax, often matched by your employer. Set and forget, and it adds up to habitat.
